terms.latin: Fac, quī ego sum, esse tē.
terms.gloss: put yourself in my place: suppose that you are who I am
terms.grammar: fac, “suppose”, with the accusative and infinitive
evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.23.1: fac, quaesō, quī ego sum, esse tē (Lewis & Short s.v. faciō)
Traupman 106: put yourself in my place, fac quī ego sum, esse tē
Traupman 107: please put yourself in my shoes, fac, quaesō, quī ego sum, tē esse
terms.comment: The imperative fac here means “suppose, imagine”: “suppose that you are the man I am”.

sources: Lewis & Short: facio
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 106–107, each phrase checked against the searchable text of the book.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
